mildly down biased in finite samples, but in the stated arbitrarily large-sample limit the loss probability vanishes for Watterson while the allele-frequency attenuation for π does not. This is the classic robustness of S to random missingness vs sensitivity of π to reference imputation.

Colleagues split on finite vs asymptotic interpretation: B supporters [1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18] argue asymptotic unbiasedness of θ_W; C supporters [13,14,2,5] emphasise finite-sample loss of rare variants and systematic reference enrichment. E[p̂]= r p

and on a site the observed heterozygosity is 2r p[1−r p] < 2p(1−p). Hence any frequency-dependent average is attenuated by the reference imputation and the attenuation persists as n→∞. 16.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core mechanism is per-haplotype random loss of a derived call with probability m>0 followed by reference imputation. For a true derived frequency p,
E[Y]= (1-m)p < p . 
Observed allele frequency is thinned by 1-m.

pi: per site heterozygosity is 2 p_obs(1-p_obs) with p_obs=(1-m)p in expectation. 
2(1-m)p[1-(1-m)p] < 2p(1-p) for the usual p range, and 
E[π_obs]=E_p[2(1-m)p(1-(1-m)p)] < E_p[2p(1-p)].
The attenuation is frequency dependent and does not vanish with n. Even as n→∞ the factor 1-m stays, so π is systematically downward biased on the VCF site set. This is agreed by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18.

Watterson: θ_W = S / a_n depends only on presence/absence of a derived allele. For a site with k=2np true derived copies,
P[site lost after imputation | k]= m^{k}.
For any fixed p>0, m^{k}=m^{2np} →0 as n→∞. Hence with arbitrarily large phased samples
S_obs → S_true in probability, and E[S_obs]=θ a_n - θ∑f^{k}/k = θ a_n - O(1).
The O(1) loss of the rarest sites is o(a_n) ~ o(log n), so S_obs/a_n → θ. Up to the common VCF ascertainment to variable sites, the segregating-site count is asymptotically recovered. That is the robustness of S to random MCAR loss vs the sensitivity of π to allele-frequency distortion.

Disagreement in the room: Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue both estimators are biased, essentially retaining a finite-n argument that rare variants can lose all their unfiltered copies and that reference imputation systematically depletes S. Colleague 8 even claims only θ is biased. The finite-n bias for Watterson is real: E[S_obs]=∑θ/k[1-f^{k}] = θ a_n - θ∑f^{k}/k, so for any finite n there is a downward O(1) bias. The question explicitly says “the number of samples is arbitrarily large”, which pushes the analysis to the n→∞ limit where the loss probability for any p>0 vanishes.

Thus on the ascertained union site set, in the stated large-sample limit, θ_W is asymptotically unbiased while π remains persistently downward biased by the 1-m thinning of allele frequencies. Majority position B. C would be the finite-sample statement.

4.text: PRIVATE REFLECTION: The pipeline is MCAR per-haplotype loss with reference imputation. Let per-haplotype loss prob be f>0, retention r=1-f, and for a true derived frequency p the imputed frequency is p̂ with E[p̂|p]=r p. The VCF site set is the union of true segregating sites, with the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples” condition. Presence/absence vs frequency: * A site is scored as segregating after imputation iff at least one true derived copy survives the filter. For k=2np true derived copies, Pr[site lost|k]=f^{k}. Hence E[S_obs]= Σ_i [1-f^{k_i}]. With the infinite-sites spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k, E[S_obs]=θ a_n - θ Σ_{k≥1} f^{k}/k. Σ f^{k}/k = -log(1-f) <∞. So θ̂_W^{obs}=S_obs/a_n = θ[1 - (Σ f^{k}/k)/a_n] → θ as n→∞. Relative bias →0; the O(1) absolute loss of the very rarest sites is o(a_n). In the arbitrarily large n limit the number of segregating sites is recovered w.h.p. and Watterson depends only on presence/absence, so the reference imputation does not change the segregation status asymptotically. * Pairwise diversity is frequency weighted. On a site E[2p̂(1-p̂)|p]=2rp(1-rp) < 2p(1-p) for 00, which is the source of the “both biased” claims. The disagreement between colleagues is essentially finite-sample absolute bias vs asymptotic relative bias; with the stated arbitrarily large sample the usual textbook statement is that S/ a_n is robust to random missing-as-reference while π is not. I am leaning to B. Only pi biased in the limit; both are downward biased for any finite n.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core mechanism is per-haplotype random thinning of derived alleles with reference imputation for the missing calls.

Let per-haplotype loss probability be $m>0$, retention $r=1-m$. For a true derived frequency $p>0$ on the ascertained SNV set

$E[\hat p\mid p]=r p$,

so the imputed allele is $Y=X B$ with $B\sim{\rm Bern}(r)$. 
For a pair of haplotypes $E[1_{\{Y_1\neq Y_2\}}]=2rp(1-rp)<2p(1-p)$. Hence per site heterozygosity is attenuated to $2rp(1-rp)$ and the sample mean $\pi_{\rm obs}$ converges to $E_p[2rp(1-rp)]\neq E_p[2p(1-p)]$. The attenuation persists as $n\to\infty$ because $r<1$ is a fixed per-sample filter. That is a systematic downward bias of nucleotide diversity.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence. A true segregating site with $k=2np$ derived copies is seen as monomorphic after imputation iff all $k$ copies are filtered: $\Pr[{\rm lost}\mid p]=m^{k}$. For any fixed $p>0$, $m^{2np}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. Hence $S_{\rm obs}\xrightarrow{P}S_{\rm true}$ on the union SNV set and $\hat\theta_W=S_{\rm obs}/a_n\to S_{\rm true}/a_n$. The $O(1)$ loss $\theta\sum f^k/k$ is $o(a_n)$, so the relative bias of $\theta_W$ vanishes in the arbitrarily large sample limit. Finite-$n$ there is a small downward loss of the rarest $k=1$ sites, but it disappears asymptotically.

Thus on the ascertained variant set $\theta_W$ is asymptotically unbiased for the presence/absence information while $\pi$ remains systematically depressed by the $(1-m)$ thinning. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition guarantees the site set is the true segregating set; genome-wide ascertainment bias to variable sites is common to both.

Disagreement in the room: colleagues 13,14,2,5 argue both statistics are downward biased because reference imputation can erase a site when all its carriers are filtered. Colleagues 1,10,11,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 show the loss probability tends to zero with $n\to\infty$ and isolate the persistent frequency attenuation of $\pi$. Colleague 8 reverses the claim. The majority asymptotic argument supports only $\pi$ being biased; $\theta_W$ is robust to random MCAR loss with reference imputation in the large-$n$ limit. The finite-sample downward bias of $S$ is noted but vanishes relative to $a_n$.

Current belief: B. Only pi is biased by the reference imputation; Watterson’s estimator is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set for arbitrarily large $n$.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The pipeline is MCAR per-haplotype loss of derived calls with reference imputation for every missing call. Let per-haplotype retention = r = 1-f, 0<r<1, f>0. For a true derived frequency p>0

E[p_obs] = r p ,   p_obs = p if the call is kept else 0.

Hence per site heterozygosity is attenuated

E[2p_obs(1-p_obs)] = 2 r p [1- r p] < 2p(1-p)

and the attenuation persists as n→∞. Pairwise diversity is a frequency-weighted statistic, so the reference imputation systematically shrinks allele frequencies toward zero and

E[π_obs] = E_p[2 r p(1- r p)] < E_p[2p(1-p)] = π_true.

The bias is downward and does not vanish with sample size.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence of polymorphism. On the VCF union set a site with k=2np true derived copies is seen as segregating after imputation with probability 1- f^k. With the stated MCAR loss

E[S_obs] = Σ_k E[N_k] [1- f^k] = θ Σ_{k≥1} k^{-1}[1- f^k] = θ a_n - θ Σ f^k/k.

Σ f^k/k = -log(1-f) <∞.  a_n = Σ_{k=1}^{2n-1}1/k ~ log n →∞.  Hence

S_obs / a_n = θ[1 - ( -log r)/a_n] → θ

in probability, and P{site lost | p>0}= f^{2np} →0 for every fixed p>0. With arbitrarily many phased haplotypes the chance that all carriers of a truly segregating site are simultaneously filtered out can be made arbitrarily small, so on the ascertained SNV set S_obs → S_true in probability. The usual O(1) loss of the very rarest k=O(1) sites is o(a_n).

Thus on the site set that is actually analysed the segregating-site count, and hence θ_W = S/a_n, is asymptotically recovered by the reference imputation, whereas the allele-frequency distortion produced by imputing missing derived alleles as reference makes π persistently downward biased.

The majority of colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 give this asymptotic robustness of S vs sensitivity of π. The “both biased” camp 13,14,2,5,9 emphasizes the finite-n loss of rare variants and the systematic reference enrichment; that loss is O(1) and vanishes relatively as n→∞, but remains a finite-sample downward bias. Colleague 8’s “only θ biased” reverses the frequency vs presence/absence distinction.

Conditional on the VCF ascertainment to polymorphic sites both statistics are upwardly ascertained relative to the whole genome, but the imputation step creates a frequency-dependent downward bias for π with essentially no first-order effect on S in the arbitrarily large sample limit. Current best reading is B: only π is biased by the reference imputation, θ_W is asymptotically unbiased for the ascertained site set.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The pipeline is MCAR per-haplotype loss of derived calls with reference imputation for the missing calls. Let f>0 be the per-haplotype per-site filtering probability, r=1-f retention. True derived frequency p>0.

Imputed allele frequency: E[p̂|p]=r p, reference alleles are never turned into derived. Hence per site observed heterozygosity

E[2 p̂(1-p̂)]=2 r p[1- r p] <2p(1-p)

for 0<p<1, with equality only at r=1. The thinning is independent of n, so the attenuation persists as n→∞. In the rare-site regime E[π̂]≈r E[π], and generally E[π̂]=E_p[2rp(1-rp)]≠E_p[2p(1-p)]. So nucleotide diversity is systematically downward biased by reference imputation, the bias is a frequency-dependent attenuation.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence. A true segregating site with k=2np true derived copies in the sample is observed as monomorphic after imputation iff all k copies are filtered: Pr[lost|k]=f^k. For any fixed p>0, k→∞ as n→∞ and f^k→0. With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the analysed site set is the union of true segregating sites. Hence

Pr[site seen as segregating|p>0]=1-f^k→1

and S_obs→S_true in probability, S_obs/a_n→θ_W,true on the ascertained variant site set. The O(1) loss -θ Σ f^k/k is o(a_n) and vanishes relative to log n. The presence/absence information is asymptotically recovered; the only remaining systematic effect is the common ascertainment to variable sites.

Thus on the VCF site set, and in the arbitrarily large n limit stated, θ_W is asymptotically unbiased by the random loss+reference imputation, while π remains persistently downward biased. The finite-n rare-variant tail gives a small downward finite-sample bias in S, which is the source of the “both biased’’ claims, but it vanishes as n→∞. The “only θ_W biased’’ claim inverts the frequency vs presence/absence distinction.

Preferred answer is B, with the caveat that both statistics share the upward ascertainment bias to the variant-only site set, and finite samples give a small downward bias in θ_W from f^k loss.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The pipeline is MCAR per-haplotype loss of a fraction f>0 of true derived calls per sample, followed by reference imputation. For a true derived frequency p>0 the imputed frequency is p_obs = (1-f)p in expectation: a derived copy is kept with prob 1-f and is turned into reference with prob f, reference copies are never turned into derived. Hence per site

E[π_i,obs]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)=π_i,true

and the downward attenuation persists as n→∞. The pairwise-difference average is frequency-weighted so reference imputation systematically depresses heterozygosity; with f>0 the bias is non-vanishing in the limit.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence of polymorphism. On the VCF union set a true segregating site with k=2np true derived copies is seen as monomorphic after imputation iff all k copies are filtered: Pr[loss|p]=f^k. For fixed p>0, f^k = f^{2np} →0 as n→∞. With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the union set is the true set of segregating SNVs and

Pr[site is segregating in imputed data|p]=1-f^k →1.

Hence S_obs → S_true in probability, S_obs/a_n → S_true/a_n and θ_W is asymptotically recovered on the ascertained SNV set. Formally E[S_obs]=θ Σ 1/k[1-f^k]=θ a_n -θ Σ f^k/k with Σ f^k/k→ -log(1-f)=O(1), so the O(1) loss is o(a_n). In finite n the rarest sites give a small downward bias in S and θ_W, but the bias vanishes relative to a_n as the sample is made arbitrarily large. 

Thus on the ascertained variant-only site set the frequency attenuation biases π persistently downward while the segregating-site count, and hence Watterson’s θ, is asymptotically unbiased. The usual upward ascertainment to polymorphic sites is common to both statistics and is not created by the imputation step.

Disagreement in the room is about whether the finite-sample rare-variant loss should be called a bias for θ_W. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,9 argue both statistics are downward biased in any finite realisation because rare variants can lose all carriers; colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 argue the loss probability →0 for arbitrarily large n and θ_W is asymptotically unbiased, π remains systematically biased. The dominant asymptotic statement is only π biased.

E[p̂]=r p,

18.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The site set that is ever analysed is the union VCF set of segregating SNVs. After quality filtering a true derived copy is retained with per-haplotype probability r = 1−m >0 and is imputed as reference with probability m, independently across haplotypes; reference copies are never lost.

Let k_i be the true number of derived copies at site i in 2n haplotypes. After imputation

Pr[site i is observed monomorphic | k_i] = m^{k_i},  
Pr[site i is observed segregating | k_i] = 1−m^{k_i}.

Hence on the VCF set

E[S_obs] = Σ_i [1−m^{k_i}],   
E[ p̂_i | p_i ] = r p_i ,   
E[ 2 p̂_i(1−p̂_i) | p_i ] = 2 r p_i [1−r p_i] < 2 p_i(1−p_i).

For a fixed p>0, k_i = 2n p →∞, so m^{k_i} →0 and a truly segregating site is seen as segregating with probability →1 as n→∞. Under the infinite-sites spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k,

E[S_obs]= θ Σ_{k≥1} (1−m^k)/k = θ a_{2n} −θ Σ m^k/k,  
Σ m^k/k = −log(1−m) <∞.

Thus S_obs/a_n = θ[1−(−log r)/a_n+o(1)] → θ, i.e. Watterson’s θ_W is asymptotically recovered on the ascertained VCF set. The O(1) loss θ Σ m^k/k is o(a_n). Finite-n the loss is a small downward bias for the very rare k=O(1) tail, which vanishes in the n→∞ limit stated in the question.

Pairwise diversity is frequency weighted. The observed per-site heterozygosity is 2 r p(1−r p) instead of 2 p(1−p); in the usual rare-site regime it is ≈2 r p. The mean over the site frequency spectrum remains

E[π_obs] = E_p[2 r p(1−r p)] < E_p[2 p(1−p)] = π_true,

with the attenuation factor r persisting in the n→∞ limit. The reference imputation therefore systematically depresses allele frequencies and heterozygosity at every site, so π is consistently downward biased even with arbitrarily many samples.

This matches the majority view that θ_W is essentially robust to random, allele-independent loss with reference imputation, while π is not. The dissenting “both biased” arguments refer to the finite-sample O(1) loss of segregating sites, m^k>0 for k=O(1), which is real for any finite n but is o(log n) and disappears in the arbitrarily large sample limit imposed here. The usual VCF ascertainment to polymorphic sites is a shared upward bias for both statistics and is not created by the imputation step.

Current best interpretation: asymptotically only nucleotide diversity is biased downward by reference imputation; Watterson’s estimator is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained site set. That is answer B, with the finite-sample caveat that both are mildly downward biased for realistic n.

For any fixed p>0, k→∞ as n→∞ and f^k→0. With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the analysed site set is the union of true segregating sites. Hence

Pr[site seen as segregating|p>0]=1-f^k→1

and S_obs→S_true in probability, S_obs/a_n→θ_W,true on the ascertained variant site set. The O(1) loss -θ Σ f^k/k is o(a_n) and vanishes relative to log n. The presence/absence information is asymptotically recovered; the only remaining systematic effect is the common ascertainment to variable sites.

Thus on the VCF site set, and in the arbitrarily large n limit stated, θ_W is asymptotically unbiased by the random loss+reference imputation, while π remains persistently downward biased. The finite-n rare-variant tail gives a small downward finite-sample bias in S, which is the source of the “both biased’’ claims, but it vanishes as n→∞. The “only θ_W biased’’ claim inverts the frequency vs presence/absence distinction.

Preferred answer is B, with the caveat that both statistics share the upward ascertainment bias to the variant-only site set, and finite samples give a small downward bias in θ_W from f^k loss.
reflection_text.12:
The pipeline is MCAR per-haplotype loss of a fraction f>0 of true derived calls per sample, followed by reference imputation. For a true derived frequency p>0 the imputed frequency is p_obs = (1-f)p in expectation: a derived copy is kept with prob 1-f and is turned into reference with prob f, reference copies are never turned into derived. Hence per site

E[π_i,obs]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)=π_i,true

and the downward attenuation persists as n→∞. The pairwise-difference average is frequency-weighted so reference imputation systematically depresses heterozygosity; with f>0 the bias is non-vanishing in the limit.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence of polymorphism. On the VCF union set a true segregating site with k=2np true derived copies is seen as monomorphic after imputation iff all k copies are filtered: Pr[loss|p]=f^k. For fixed p>0, f^k = f^{2np} →0 as n→∞. With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the union set is the true set of segregating SNVs and

Pr[site is segregating in imputed data|p]=1-f^k →1.

Hence S_obs → S_true in probability, S_obs/a_n → S_true/a_n and θ_W is asymptotically recovered on the ascertained SNV set. Formally E[S_obs]=θ Σ 1/k[1-f^k]=θ a_n -θ Σ f^k/k with Σ f^k/k→ -log(1-f)=O(1), so the O(1) loss is o(a_n). In finite n the rarest sites give a small downward bias in S and θ_W, but the bias vanishes relative to a_n as the sample is made arbitrarily large. 

Thus on the ascertained variant-only site set the frequency attenuation biases π persistently downward while the segregating-site count, and hence Watterson’s θ, is asymptotically unbiased. The usual upward ascertainment to polymorphic sites is common to both statistics and is not created by the imputation step.

Disagreement in the room is about whether the finite-sample rare-variant loss should be called a bias for θ_W. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,9 argue both statistics are downward biased in any finite realisation because rare variants can lose all carriers; colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 argue the loss probability →0 for arbitrarily large n and θ_W is asymptotically unbiased, π remains systematically biased. The dominant asymptotic statement is only π biased.

reflection_text.17:
The site set analysed is the union VCF of segregating SNVs, with the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples” condition. After per-sample quality filtering a fraction f>0 of true derived calls is removed at random per haplotype and every missing call is imputed as reference. The reference allele is never lost, the derived allele is kept with probability r=1−f.

For a true haploid derived frequency p>0
E[p̂]=r p,
so the per-site heterozygosity is attenuated to
2p̂(1−p̂)=2rp[1−rp] < 2p(1−p)
with strict inequality for 0<p<1. Pairwise differences are therefore systematically depressed. The attenuation factor r persists as n→∞, so nucleotide diversity π is asymptotically downward biased under reference imputation. This is the usual frequency-dependent effect.

Watterson’s estimator uses only presence/absence of polymorphism, θW=S/a_n. A site with k=2np true derived copies is seen as segregating after imputation iff at least one copy survives filtering, probability 1−r^{k}. With k fixed,
Pr[site lost|k]=r^{k}<1,
and for any fixed p>0, k→∞ as n→∞ so Pr[site lost|p]=r^{k}→0. In expectation

E[S_obs]=∑_k θ/k [1−r^{k}] = θ a_n −θ∑_k r^{k}/k,

so the O(1) loss ∑ r^{k}/k is o(a_n). Hence S_obs/a_n→θ in probability as n→∞, i.e. the segregating-site count and Watterson’s θ are asymptotically recovered for the ascertained VCF site set. The only remaining systematic effect is the common VCF ascertainment to variable sites.

Hence in the arbitrarily large sample limit the presence/absence information used by θW is essentially preserved while the frequency information used by π is permanently shrunk by the r factor. The finite-n downward loss of the rarest k=O(1) sites gives a small O(1) finite-sample bias of θW, but it vanishes relatively as n→∞. Majority of colleagues argue B, only π biased; the minority C argument stresses the finite-sample loss of very rare variants and the systematic reference enrichment. With the stated n→∞ limit the asymptotic statement is only π biased.
reflection_text.18:
The site set that is ever analysed is the union VCF set of segregating SNVs. After quality filtering a true derived copy is retained with per-haplotype probability r = 1−m >0 and is imputed as reference with probability m, independently across haplotypes; reference copies are never lost.

Let k_i be the true number of derived copies at site i in 2n haplotypes. After imputation

Pr[site i is observed monomorphic | k_i] = m^{k_i},  
Pr[site i is observed segregating | k_i] = 1−m^{k_i}.

Hence on the VCF set

E[S_obs] = Σ_i [1−m^{k_i}],   
E[ p̂_i | p_i ] = r p_i ,   
E[ 2 p̂_i(1−p̂_i) | p_i ] = 2 r p_i [1−r p_i] < 2 p_i(1−p_i).

For a fixed p>0, k_i = 2n p →∞, so m^{k_i} →0 and a truly segregating site is seen as segregating with probability →1 as n→∞. Under the infinite-sites spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k,

E[S_obs]= θ Σ_{k≥1} (1−m^k)/k = θ a_{2n} −θ Σ m^k/k,  
Σ m^k/k = −log(1−m) <∞.

Thus S_obs/a_n = θ[1−(−log r)/a_n+o(1)] → θ, i.e. Watterson’s θ_W is asymptotically recovered on the ascertained VCF set. The O(1) loss θ Σ m^k/k is o(a_n). Finite-n the loss is a small downward bias for the very rare k=O(1) tail, which vanishes in the n→∞ limit stated in the question.

Pairwise diversity is frequency weighted. The observed per-site heterozygosity is 2 r p(1−r p) instead of 2 p(1−p); in the usual rare-site regime it is ≈2 r p. The mean over the site frequency spectrum remains

E[π_obs] = E_p[2 r p(1−r p)] < E_p[2 p(1−p)] = π_true,

with the attenuation factor r persisting in the n→∞ limit. The reference imputation therefore systematically depresses allele frequencies and heterozygosity at every site, so π is consistently downward biased even with arbitrarily many samples.

This matches the majority view that θ_W is essentially robust to random, allele-independent loss with reference imputation, while π is not. The dissenting “both biased” arguments refer to the finite-sample O(1) loss of segregating sites, m^k>0 for k=O(1), which is real for any finite n but is o(log n) and disappears in the arbitrarily large sample limit imposed here. The usual VCF ascertainment to polymorphic sites is a shared upward bias for both statistics and is not created by the imputation step.

Current best interpretation: asymptotically only nucleotide diversity is biased downward by reference imputation; Watterson’s estimator is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained site set. That is answer B, with the finite-sample caveat that both are mildly downward biased for realistic n.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The reference fill-in is a systematic one way loss of derived alleles and that loss hits both the count of segregating sites and the frequency weighted average.

Let f>0 be the per haplotype per site probability that a true derived call is filtered out and then replaced by the reference. On a true biallelic site with true derived frequency p the imputed allele is observed as derived only when the call is retained. Hence 
E[ p̂ | p ] = (1-f)p < p
and the observed heterozygosity at the site is 
2p̂(1-p̂)=2(1-f)p[1-(1-f)p] < 2p(1-p)
for every 0<p<1. The pairwise difference, and therefore π, is a non linear function of p and is therefore deflated at every site by the (1-f) thinning. The deflation does not vanish with n because the thinning operates on every haplotype independently of sample size. So π_obs is systematically < π_true under the described pipeline.

The same thinning also changes the presence/absence information that Watterson uses. A site with k true derived copies in the sample is seen as segregating after imputation only if at least one of those k copies is retained, i.e. with probability 1-f^{k}. Under the infinite sites model E[N_k]=θ/k so

E[S_obs]= Σ_k θ/k [1-f^{k}] = θ a_n - θ Σ_k f^{k}/k

The loss term θ Σ_k f^{k}/k = θ[-log(1-f)] is O(1). With an arbitrarily large number of phased haplotypes a_n diverges like log n, so the relative loss of S goes to zero, but the absolute number of sites that are turned into apparent reference/reference by reference imputation stays positive. In practice the site spectrum is dominated by the rare tail k = O(1) singletons, doubletons etc. For any fixed k, Pr[site lost | k]=f^{k}>0 and does not depend on n. Because the VCF is ascertained to sites that are polymorphic somewhere in the panel, and a substantial minority of calls are then removed per sample at random, rare variants can and do lose all of their unfiltered derived copies in the realised data set and are imputed as monomorphic reference in every haplotype. The ‘no completely missing SNV across all samples’ condition refers to the original VCFs, not to the per-sample filtered and reference-filled alignments that are actually analysed.

Hence the observed S is a downward realisation of the true number of segregating sites on the ascertained set, and θ_W = S/a_n is also a systematic underestimate. The reference imputation makes the data reference enriched at every site, so both the segregating site count used by Watterson and the allele-frequency weighted pairwise difference used by π are biased downwards. The asymptotic k_n=2np →∞ argument only applies to sites with fixed p>0, it does not remove the persistent f^{k}>0 loss for the k=O(1) rare variant tail that dominates S. On the site set actually analysed both statistics are therefore biased.

1.text:
The two statistics react differently to a random per-haplotype thinning followed by deterministic reference imputation. Let $f>0$ be the per haplotype per site probability that a true derived call is filtered out and $r=1-f$ the retention probability. On a true segregating site with true haploid frequency $p>0$ $$ E[\hat p\mid p]=r p

0$ true derived copies $$ \Pr\{{\rm site\;lost\;after\;imputation}\mid k\}=f^{\,k}, $$ i.e. the site is seen as monomorphic only if all $k$ copies are filtered. With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the union site set is the true segregating set. For any fixed $p>0$, $k\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and $$ f^{\,k}=f^{\,2np}\to0, \qquad\Pr\{{\rm site\;segregating}\mid p\}=1-f^{k}\to1. $$ Hence $$ E[S_{\rm obs}]=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\theta}{k}\,[1-f^{k}] =\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{f^{k}}{k}, $$ with $\sum_{k}f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)=O(1)$ while $a_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{2n-1}1/k\sim \log n$. Thus $$ \frac{S_{\rm obs}}{a_{n}}=\theta+o_{p}(1),\qquad n\to\infty, $$ so on the ascertained VCF site set $\hat\theta_{W}=S_{\rm obs}/a_{n}$ is asymptotically recovered. The $O(1)$ loss $-\theta\sum f^{k}/k$ is a finite sample downward bias that is $o(a_{n})$ and disappears in the arbitrarily large sample limit. The ordinary VCF ascertainment to variable sites biases both $\theta_{W}$ and $\pi$ upwards relative to the whole genome, but that bias is common to the two statistics and is not created by the missing-as-reference imputation step. Conditional on the VCF site set, $\theta_{W}$ is first-order robust to random loss of genotypes whereas the frequency-weighted $\pi$ is systematically depressed by the $r$ attenuation of allele frequencies. That is the usual missing-as-reference bias: $\pi$ is persistently downward biased, $\theta_{W}$ is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained site set. In finite $n$ there is a small $O(1)$ downward bias in $S$ as well.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I keep coming back to the per-site loss probability, because it’s what the reference imputation actually does.

For a true segregating site with k true derived copies in the sample, after per-haplotype quality filtering with per-copy loss probability f>0 the number of derived copies that survive is Bin(k,1-f). The imputed sequence is monomorphic at that site iff K_obs=0, i.e. iff

P[site appears monomorphic | k] = f^k >0

and the observed derived frequency conditional on k is (1-f)k/2n. The reference allele is never lost, so the imputation is a one-way thinning of derived alleles.

That thinning is obvious for π. The observed per-site heterozygosity is 2 p_obs(1-p_obs) with p_obs=(1-f)p in expectation, so

E[2 p_obs(1-p_obs)] = 2(1-f)p[1-(1-f)p] < 2p(1-p)

for every 0<p<1. The pairwise difference average is therefore systematically depressed and the depression does not disappear as n grows; the allele-frequency shrinkage by 1-f persists.

The same thinning hits S. On the ascertained union set of true SNVs

E[S_obs] = Σ_i [1 - f^{k_i}] = Σ_k E[N_k] [1 - f^k] ,

with E[N_k]=θ/k under infinite sites. Hence

E[S_obs] = θ Σ_k (1-f^k)/k = θ a_n - θ Σ_k f^k/k .

The loss probability f^k is >0 for every finite k, and the infinite-sites spectrum always contains an infinite tail of k = O(1) sites. A rare variant carried by one or two haplotypes can be completely filtered out in the samples that carry it, and once filtered it is imputed as reference in every haplotype.

That is exactly what colleagues 13,14,2 and 5 are pointing to: reference fill-in is systematic reference enrichment. A site can be present in the union VCF, satisfy “no completely missing SNV across all samples” pre-filter, and still become monomorphic after sample-specific deletions are replaced by reference. The expected segregating-site count is therefore < the true segregating-site count on the analysed set, and θ_W = S_obs/a_n inherits that downward bias.

The m^{2np} →0 argument is only for a fixed frequency p>0. For p scaling as c/2n, k=c=O(1) and f^k stays bounded away from zero. In practice the rare-variant tail dominates the site count, so the O(1) loss in S is real and both S-based and frequency-based summaries are downward biased by the reference imputation. The usual “θ_W is robust” statement is an asymptotic relative statement; in absolute expectation both Watterson and π are underestimates under the described pipeline.

are never lost.

For a true haploid derived frequency $p>0$ with $k=2np$ true derived
copies in $n$ diploids

$E[\hat p\mid p]=(1-f)p$,

because a derived copy is seen iff it is not filtered, and a reference
copy is never turned into derived.  Hence for the site

$E[\hat\pi_i\mid p]=2\hat p(1-\hat p)=2(1-f)p[1-(1-f)p]

Hence

$E[\hat\pi]=E_{p\in M}\!\left[2(1-f)p\bigl(1-(1-f)p\bigr)\right]
<E_{p\in M}[2p(1-p)]$,

so the average pairwise difference is systematically attenuated by the
reference imputation.  The bias persists in the $n\to\infty$ limit; it is
a frequency-dependent bias.

Presence/absence is different.  Conditional on $k$ true derived copies
$K_{o}\mid k\sim{\rm Bin}(k,1-f)$ and

$P\{\hbox{site is seen as monomorphic}\mid k\}=f^{\,k}$.

infinite-sites spectrum $E[N_k]=\theta/k$,

$E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\theta}{k}\left[1-f^{k}\right]
 =\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k$,
$\sum_{k}f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)<\infty$.

$\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}
 =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum_{k}f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]
 \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{p}\theta$

on the $M$ site set.  The $O(1)$ loss $ \theta\sum f^{k}/k$ is $o(a_{n})=o(\log n)$,

the loss is $O(1)$ whereas $a_{n}\sim\log n\to\infty$.  In the arbitrarily
large-sample limit

$$ \frac{S_{obs}}{a_{n}}=\theta_{W}^{obs}
   =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]\xrightarrow{p}\theta,
$$

i.e. on the ascertained SNV set $S_{obs}\xrightarrow{p}S_{true}$ and
$\theta_{W}^{obs}$ is asymptotically recovered.  The segregating-site
count is therefore first-order robust to random, allele-independent loss
followed by reference imputation, whereas the allele-frequency distortion

statistics; conditional on the VCF site set the imputation step biases

4.text:
With the VCF site set taken as the union of true segregating sites the
filtering is per haplotype MCAR with retention $r=1-f>0$ and reference
imputation

$Y_{i}=X_{i}{\bf1}_{\rm obs}$,  $ {\mathbb E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}]=rX_{i}$ ,

so that for a site with true derived frequency $p>0$

${\mathbb E}[\hat p\mid p]=rp<p$ .

* Segregation

A true site with $k=2np$ derived copies in the sample is seen as
segregating after imputation iff $K_{o}>0$ with $K_{o}\mid k\sim{\rm Bin}(k,r)$.
Hence

${\rm Pr}\{\hbox{site lost}\mid k\}=f^{\,k},\qquad
{\mathbb E}[S_{o}]=\sum_{i}\bigl[1-f^{\,k_{i}}\bigr]$.

On the infinite-sites spectrum ${\mathbb E}[N_{k}]=\theta/k$

${\mathbb E}[S_{o}]=\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k$,

$\sum_{k}f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)<\infty$, and

$\hat\theta_{W}^{o}=S_{o}/a_{n}
 =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum_{k}f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\theta$.

ascertainment to variable sites the presence/absence information on which

as the sample is made arbitrarily large; in finite $n$ it is a small
downward $O(1/\log n)$ term.

* Pairwise diversity

${\mathbb E}[2\hat p(1-\hat p)\mid p]=2rp(1-rp)<2p(1-p)$ for $0<p<1$, and
with $p\ll1$ ${\mathbb E}[2\hat p(1-\hat p)\mid p]\simeq2rp$.
Hence on the ascertained site set

${\mathbb E}[\pi_{o}]={\mathbb E}_{p}[2rp(1-rp)]<{\mathbb E}_{p}[2p(1-p)]
=\pi_{\rm true},$

and in the rare-site limit ${\mathbb E}[\pi_{o}]\approx r\,\pi_{\rm true}$.
The $r$ attenuation of the observed allele frequencies persists as

reference, depressing heterozygosity and pairwise differences by a
non-vanishing factor $r$, $1-f^{2}$ etc.

unbiased under random per-sample loss with reference imputation, whereas
$\pi$ is systematically downward biased by the allele-frequency shrinkage
$p\mapsto rp$. The usual VCF ascertainment bias to polymorphic sites is
common to both statistics. This is the classic robustness of $S$ to random
missing-as-reference versus the sensitivity of $\pi$ to frequency
distortion.

With that pipeline a rare variant carried by only a few haplotypes can lose all of its unfiltered copies in the realised sample and be imputed as reference/reference in the constructed alignment. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples” condition is pre-filter; after per-sample deletion + reference imputation a site can become monomorphic in the final sequences.

Hence in any calculation that is actually performed S_obs is stochastically smaller than the true number of segregating sites on the union VCF set, and θW = S_obs/a_n inherits a downward bias in addition to the downward bias of π. The familiar asymptotic robustness of S to random loss is a limit result; with a finite, however large, sample the reference imputation systematically enriches the alignments for the reference allele and both the site-count and the frequency-weighted statistics are underestimates. That is the usual both-biased operational conclusion for missing-as-reference imputation.

10.text:
The data that go into the two summaries are the same imputed alignments.
Let $m>0$ be the per-haplotype per-site probability that a true derived
call is lost by the quality filter and let the lost call be imputed to the
reference. For a true derived allele with population frequency $p>0$

* $Y_{i}=X_{i}{\bf 1}_{\rm obs}$ with ${\mathbb E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=1]=1-m$,
so that on the ascertained VCF site set

${\mathbb E}[\hat p\mid p]=(1-m)p<p$,

the reference state is never created.  Hence for a site

${\mathbb E}\big[\,2\hat p(1-\hat p)\mid p\big]
 =2(1-m)p\Big[1-(1-m)p\Big]
 <2p(1-p)$

for every $0<p<1$.  With random independent loss per haplotype

$\hat\pi
 =\frac1L\sum_{\ell}2\hat p_{\ell}(1-\hat p_{\ell})
 \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{p}
 {\mathbb E}_{p}\!\left[2(1-m)p\big(1-(1-m)p\big)\right]
 <{\mathbb E}_{p}\!\left[2p(1-p)\right]=\pi_{\rm true}$,

i.e. the pairwise difference spectrum is attenuated by the $1-m$
thinning of the derived allele frequency.  The attenuation
$2p(1-m)\big[1-(1-m)p\big]$ persists for $n\to\infty$, so $\pi$ is
persistently downward biased by the reference fill-in. For rare sites
${\mathbb E}[\hat\pi_{\ell}]\simeq2(1-m)p$ and for the usual
human $p$ range the bias is $\simeq1-m^{2}$.

Watterson uses only presence/absence.  A true segregating site with
$k_{n}=2np$ true derived copies in a sample of $n$ diploids is declared
monomorphic after imputation iff all $k_{n}$ copies are filtered:

${\Pr}\big\{{\rm site\;lost}\mid p\big\}=m^{k_{n}}=m^{2np}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0$
for every fixed $p>0$.
With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the
union site set is the true segregating set ${\cal S}_{T}$. Hence

${\mathbb E}[S_{\rm obs}]
 =\sum_{i\in{\cal S}_{T}}\Big[1-m^{k_{i}}\Big]
 =S_{\rm true}-\sum_{i}m^{k_{i}},\qquad
\sum_{i}m^{k_{i}}=O(1)$,

so that

$\hat\theta_{W}^{\rm obs}
 =\frac{S_{\rm obs}}{a_{n}}
 =\theta\Bigg[1-\frac{\sum_{k}f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigg]
 \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{p}\theta$,

$a_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{2n-1}k^{-1}=\log n+O(1)$.
Up to the $O(1)$ loss of the very rarest $k=O(1)$ tail the number of
segregating sites, and therefore $S/a_{n}$, is recovered with probability
one in the arbitrarily large sample limit.  The $O(1)$ finite-$n$ loss
is $o(a_{n})$ and disappears relative to the $\log n$ growth of $S$.

Thus on the VCF ascertained site set the segregating-site count and
$\theta_{W}$ are asymptotically robust to MCAR loss + reference
imputation, whereas the frequency weighted pairwise average is
systematically depressed.  The well known VCF ascertainment to
polymorphic sites biases both summaries relative to a genome-wide
$\theta$ in the same way and is not created by the imputation step.

That is the usual $\theta_{W}$ robust to random loss of genotype
versus $\pi$ sensitive to allele-frequency distortion.  In finite samples
both are mildly downward biased; in the $n\to\infty$ limit stated in the
question only $\pi$ remains biased.

17.text:
For the set of sites that is actually analysed the site set is the union VCF set \({\cal S}_{V}\). Let \(r=1-f\in(0,1)\) be the per-haplotype probability that a true derived call is retained after the quality filter and let \(p>0\) be the true haploid derived frequency at a site in \({\cal S}_{V}\). After the reference fill-in \[ {\mathbb E}[\hat p\mid p]=r p

0 . \] With the “no completely missing SNV’’ condition the site set is the true segregating set \({\cal S}_{V}\). Hence \[ {\mathbb E}[S_{obs}] =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\theta}{k}\bigl[1-f^{k}\bigr] =\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k, \] so that \[ \hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n} =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum_{k}f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr] \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\theta , \] in probability. The \(O(1)\) loss \(\theta\sum f^{k}/k\) is \(o(a_{n})\) and vanishes relatively as \(n\to\infty\); in the arbitrarily large sample limit every truly segregating site is seen as segregating with probability one. Up to the common VCF ascertainment to variable sites the segregating- site count, and therefore \(\theta_{W}\), is asymptotically recovered while the frequency information on which \(\pi\) is based is permanently attenuated by the \(r\) thinning. That is the usual robustness of \(S\) to random missingness versus the sensitivity of \(\pi\) to reference imputation. In finite \(n\) the \(f^{k}\) term gives a small \(O(1)\) downward finite-sample bias of \(\theta_{W}\) as well, but in the stated \(n\to\infty\) limit the only systematic distortion introduced by the filter+reference imputation on the VCF site set is the downward bias of \(\pi\). B. Only pi (nucleotide diversity) is biased.

12.text:
With the union set of VCF sites fixed and the missing calls imputed to the
reference, the two summaries react differently to the MCAR
per-haplotype thinning.

Let $f>0$ be the per haplotype probability that a true derived call is
filtered out and let $r=1-f$. For a true derived frequency $p>0$

* observed frequency on the imputed haplotype
  $p_{o}=r\,p$ in expectation, and 
  $E[Y_{i}Y_{j}]$ is attenuated.
  The per site heterozygosity that enters $\pi$ is
  $2p_{o}\!\left(1-p_{o}\right)=2rp\!\left[1-rp\right]<2p(1-p)$.
  Hence $E[\pi_{i,o}]< \pi_{i,true}$ for every $0<p<1$ and

$$
E[\pi_{o}] =E_{p}\!\left[2rp(1-rp)\right] < E_{p}\!\left[2p(1-p)\right]
$$

for any $r<1$. The $(1-f)$ attenuation of the allele frequency is a
systematic reference bias. It persists as $n\to\infty$; $\pi$ is
consistently down shifted, $E[\pi_{o}]\to\theta(1-f^{2})<\theta$, and in
the rare-site regime $E[\pi_{o}]\simeq2r p$.

A site is scored by Watterson only on presence/absence of polymorphism.
For a true segregating site with $k_{n}=2np>0$ true derived copies

$$
\Pr\{{\rm site\;lost\mid p}\}= f^{\,k_{n}}=f^{\,2np}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0
\qquad\forall p>0 .
$$

With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the
union set is the true set of segregating SNVs, $ {\cal S}_{T}$.
Hence

$$
\Pr\{K_{o}>0\mid k\}=1-f^{k}\to1,\qquad
E[S_{o}]=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\theta}{k}\!\left[1-f^{k}\right]
       =\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{f^{k}}{k}.
$$

$\sum f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)=O(1)$ while $a_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{2n}k^{-1}
\sim\log n\to\infty$. Thus

$$
\hat\theta_{W}^{o}=S_{o}/a_{n}
   =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{P}\theta,
$$

so on the ascertained SNV set the segregating-site count, and hence
Watterson’s $\theta_{W}$, is asymptotically recovered. The $O(1)$
loss $ \theta\sum f^{k}/k$ is $o(a_{n})$ and vanishes relative to $S$
in the arbitrarily large sample limit. The usual upward ascertainment to
the variant-only site set is common to both statistics.

The frequency-dependent quantity $\pi$ is therefore the one that remains
systematically depressed by reference imputation, $\theta_{W}$ is first
order asymptotically unbiased on the VCF site set.

That is the B statement: only $\pi$ is biased, $\theta_{W}$ is
asymptotically unbiased for the ascertained sites.  The familiar finite-$n$
downward $O(1)$ loss of the rarest sites is the finite-sample bias that
is often quoted as “both biased’’ but vanishes relative to $a_{n}$ as
$n\to\infty$.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the “asymptotically unbiased for θW” line is being pushed too far and it hides the finite-sample reality that the question is actually about.

The site set we analyse is the union VCF, so every site is genuinely segregating in the population. After per-sample quality filtering a true derived copy is kept with probability 1−f and turned into a forced reference call with probability f, independently per haplotype. For a site with k true derived copies in the sample

Pr[ site is seen as segregating after imputation | k ] = 1 − f^{k}.

With the infinite-sites spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k this gives

E[S_obs]= Σ_k θ/k [1− f^{k}] = θ a_n − θ Σ_k f^{k}/k .

Σ_k f^{k}/k = −log(1−f) < ∞, so the absolute loss of segregating sites is a positive constant. The relative loss θ Σ f^{k}/k / a_n vanishes as a_n∼log n→∞, but the question says “arbitrarily large” not infinite, and the loss is  non-zero for every finite n. In particular the rare-variant tail k=O(1) never disappears: for k=1,2,… Pr[loss]=f^{k}>0 persists no matter how large n is. Those rare variants are a substantial fraction of a human VCF and they are exactly the ones that can be wiped out when the few carriers that exist happen to be the haplotypes in which the site was filtered. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples” condition is about the union before per-sample deletion; after sample-specific deletion + reference imputation a site can still be imputed as reference in every haplotype and become monomorphic in the final alignment. That makes S systematically undercounted and θ_W = S/a_n downward biased in any real data set, which is the finite-N form that Colleagues 11 and 12 already flagged.

π is affected in a different but also systematic way. The observed derived frequency is E[p̂|p]= (1−f)p, so

E[2p̂(1−p̂)] = 2(1−f)p[1−(1−f)p] < 2p(1−p)

for every 0<p<1. The reference imputation therefore thins the allele frequency spectrum at every site and depresses the pairwise difference at every site. The attenuation to (1−f) of the frequency persists as n→∞.

So we have a genuine downward reference bias for the frequency-weighted statistic π and a downward loss-of-segregating-sites bias for the presence/absence statistic θ_W. On the VCF site set both estimators are underestimates of the true diversity for the population. That is the both-biased situation argued by Colleagues 13, 14, 2, 5 and 9.

18.text:
The sites that enter the analysis are the union $M$ of sites that are
segregating in the panel and are present in at least one sample after the
per-sample quality filter.  Let $r=1-m>0$ be the per-haplotype probability
that a true derived copy is retained and let $k_{i}=2np_{i}>0$ be the true
number of derived copies at a site $i$ in $2n$ phased haplotypes.  After
reference imputation

* $K_{o,i}\mid k_{i}\sim {\rm Bin}(k_{i},r)$,
* the site is seen as segregating iff $K_{o,i}>0$,

${\rm Pr}\{ {\rm site\;lost}\mid k_{i}\}=m^{k_{i}},\qquad
{\rm Pr}\{ {\rm site\;segregating}\mid k_{i}\}=1-m^{k_{i}}  .
$

For a fixed true frequency $p_{i}>0$
$m^{k_{i}}=m^{2np_{i}}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, so

${\rm Pr}\{ {\rm site\;segregating}\mid p_{i}>0\}\to1 ,$

and with the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’
${\rm E}[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i}[1-m^{k_{i}}]\to |M|$.  Hence on the ascertained
site set $M$

$S_{obs}\xrightarrow{p}S_{true},\qquad 
\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow{p}S_{true}/a_{n},$

up to the $O(1)$ loss $\theta\sum_{k}m^{k}/k=-\theta\log r$ which is
$o(a_{n})$.  Presence/absence of polymorphism is therefore recovered in
the $n\to\infty$ limit; Watterson’s estimator is asymptotically
unbiased for the $M$ site set.  The $O(1)$ loss for the very rare
$k=O(1)$ tail is the familiar finite-$n$ downward bias, $o(\log n)$,
and disappears in the arbitrarily large sample limit imposed here.

Frequency information is not recovered.  For a haplotype
$Y = X B$ with $B\sim {\rm Bernoulli}(r)$ independent of the true allele
$X\in\{0,1\}$,
${\rm E}[Y\mid X]=rX$ and

${\rm E}[\hat p_{i}\mid p_{i}]=r p_{i}<p_{i}$.

The observed per-site heterozygosity is therefore

${\rm E}\big[\,2\hat p_{i}(1-\hat p_{i})\mid p_{i}\big]
   =2r p_{i}\big[\,1-r p_{i}\big] <2p_{i}(1-p_{i}),$

with the attenuation $r$ persisting for every $p_{i}>0$.  In the
usual rare-site regime ${\rm E}[\hat\pi_{i}]\approx2r p_{i}$ so that

${\rm E}[\pi_{obs}]
   ={\rm E}_{p}\!\left[\,2r p(1-rp)\right]
   <{\rm E}_{p}\!\left[\,2p(1-p)\right]=\pi_{true},$

and the bias $1-r^{2}$ for $p\approx1/2$ does not vanish as $n\to\infty$.
Reference imputation therefore systematically depresses observed allele
frequencies and pairwise differences at every site.

Thus on the VCF ascertained site set the segregating-site count, and
hence Watterson’s $\theta_{W}$, is asymptotically recovered by random
allele-independent loss with reference imputation, whereas nucleotide
diversity $\pi$ remains consistently downward biased by the $r$
attenuation of allele frequencies.  The shared upward ascertainment bias
from restricting to $M$ is common to both statistics and is not created
by the imputation step.  In finite samples both statistics are mildly
downward biased by the $m^{k}$ tail, i.e. the classic $O(1)$ loss of the
rarest sites.

public_text.5:
The reference fill-in is a systematic one way loss of derived alleles and that loss hits both the count of segregating sites and the frequency weighted average.

Let f>0 be the per haplotype per site probability that a true derived call is filtered out and then replaced by the reference. On a true biallelic site with true derived frequency p the imputed allele is observed as derived only when the call is retained. Hence 
E[ p̂ | p ] = (1-f)p < p
and the observed heterozygosity at the site is 
2p̂(1-p̂)=2(1-f)p[1-(1-f)p] < 2p(1-p)
for every 0<p<1. The pairwise difference, and therefore π, is a non linear function of p and is therefore deflated at every site by the (1-f) thinning. The deflation does not vanish with n because the thinning operates on every haplotype independently of sample size. So π_obs is systematically < π_true under the described pipeline.

The same thinning also changes the presence/absence information that Watterson uses. A site with k true derived copies in the sample is seen as segregating after imputation only if at least one of those k copies is retained, i.e. with probability 1-f^{k}. Under the infinite sites model E[N_k]=θ/k so

E[S_obs]= Σ_k θ/k [1-f^{k}] = θ a_n - θ Σ_k f^{k}/k

The loss term θ Σ_k f^{k}/k = θ[-log(1-f)] is O(1). With an arbitrarily large number of phased haplotypes a_n diverges like log n, so the relative loss of S goes to zero, but the absolute number of sites that are turned into apparent reference/reference by reference imputation stays positive. In practice the site spectrum is dominated by the rare tail k = O(1) singletons, doubletons etc. For any fixed k, Pr[site lost | k]=f^{k}>0 and does not depend on n. Because the VCF is ascertained to sites that are polymorphic somewhere in the panel, and a substantial minority of calls are then removed per sample at random, rare variants can and do lose all of their unfiltered derived copies in the realised data set and are imputed as monomorphic reference in every haplotype. The ‘no completely missing SNV across all samples’ condition refers to the original VCFs, not to the per-sample filtered and reference-filled alignments that are actually analysed.

Hence the observed S is a downward realisation of the true number of segregating sites on the ascertained set, and θ_W = S/a_n is also a systematic underestimate. The reference imputation makes the data reference enriched at every site, so both the segregating site count used by Watterson and the allele-frequency weighted pairwise difference used by π are biased downwards. The asymptotic k_n=2np →∞ argument only applies to sites with fixed p>0, it does not remove the persistent f^{k}>0 loss for the k=O(1) rare variant tail that dominates S. On the site set actually analysed both statistics are therefore biased.

0$ true derived copies $$ \Pr\{{\rm site\;lost\;after\;imputation}\mid k\}=f^{\,k}, $$ i.e. the site is seen as monomorphic only if all $k$ copies are filtered. public_text.8:
I keep coming back to the per-site loss probability, because it’s what the reference imputation actually does.

For a true segregating site with k true derived copies in the sample, after per-haplotype quality filtering with per-copy loss probability f>0 the number of derived copies that survive is Bin(k,1-f). The imputed sequence is monomorphic at that site iff K_obs=0, i.e. iff

P[site appears monomorphic | k] = f^k >0

and the observed derived frequency conditional on k is (1-f)k/2n. The reference allele is never lost, so the imputation is a one-way thinning of derived alleles.

That thinning is obvious for π. The observed per-site heterozygosity is 2 p_obs(1-p_obs) with p_obs=(1-f)p in expectation, so

E[2 p_obs(1-p_obs)] = 2(1-f)p[1-(1-f)p] < 2p(1-p)

for every 0<p<1. The pairwise difference average is therefore systematically depressed and the depression does not disappear as n grows; the allele-frequency shrinkage by 1-f persists.

The same thinning hits S. On the ascertained union set of true SNVs

E[S_obs] = Σ_i [1 - f^{k_i}] = Σ_k E[N_k] [1 - f^k] ,

with E[N_k]=θ/k under infinite sites. Hence

E[S_obs] = θ Σ_k (1-f^k)/k = θ a_n - θ Σ_k f^k/k .

Σ_k f^k/k = -log(1-f) < ∞, so the expected number of sites lost is a positive constant θ[-log(1-f)], not o(1) in absolute terms. The loss probability f^k is >0 for every finite k, and the infinite-sites spectrum always contains an infinite tail of k = O(1) sites. A rare variant carried by one or two haplotypes can be completely filtered out in the samples that carry it, and once filtered it is imputed as reference in every haplotype.

That is exactly what colleagues 13,14,2 and 5 are pointing to: reference fill-in is systematic reference enrichment. A site can be present in the union VCF, satisfy “no completely missing SNV across all samples” pre-filter, and still become monomorphic after sample-specific deletions are replaced by reference. The expected segregating-site count is therefore < the true segregating-site count on the analysed set, and θ_W = S_obs/a_n inherits that downward bias.

The m^{2np} →0 argument is only for a fixed frequency p>0. For p scaling as c/2n, k=c=O(1) and f^k stays bounded away from zero. In practice the rare-variant tail dominates the site count, so the O(1) loss in S is real and both S-based and frequency-based summaries are downward biased by the reference imputation. The usual “θ_W is robust” statement is an asymptotic relative statement; in absolute expectation both Watterson and π are underestimates under the described pipeline.

${\mathbb E}[Y]=rp<p$

and the $O(1)$ loss $ \theta\sum f^{k}/k$ is $o(a_{n})$.  The presence/absence
information used by $\theta_{W}$ is asymptotically recovered, the only
remaining systematic effect being the usual VCF ascertainment to variable
sites which is common to both statistics.

The VCF site set is the union of the true segregating sites.  By construction
the site is never completely absent from the panel, so on the ascertained
set $M$ we are conditioning on $p>0$.

Let $f>0$ be the per-haplotype probability that a true derived copy is
filtered out and subsequently imputed to the reference.  Reference copies
are never lost.

For a true haploid derived frequency $p>0$ with $k=2np$ true derived
copies in $n$ diploids

$E[\hat p\mid p]=(1-f)p$,

because a derived copy is seen iff it is not filtered, and a reference
copy is never turned into derived.  Hence for the site

$E[\hat\pi_i\mid p]=2\hat p(1-\hat p)=2(1-f)p[1-(1-f)p]
<2p(1-p)=\pi_{i,true}$

for every $0<p<1$, and in the rare-site regime $p\ll1$, $E[\hat\pi_i]\simeq
2(1-f)p$. The factor $1-f$ is per-haplotype and does not vanish with $n$.
Hence

$E[\hat\pi]=E_{p\in M}\!\left[2(1-f)p\bigl(1-(1-f)p\bigr)\right]
<E_{p\in M}[2p(1-p)]$,

so the average pairwise difference is systematically attenuated by the
reference imputation.  The bias persists in the $n\to\infty$ limit; it is
a frequency-dependent bias.

Presence/absence is different.  Conditional on $k$ true derived copies
$K_{o}\mid k\sim{\rm Bin}(k,1-f)$ and

$P\{\hbox{site is seen as monomorphic}\mid k\}=f^{\,k}$.

With $k=2np$, $f^{k}\to0$ for every fixed $p>0$ as $n\to\infty$.  On the
infinite-sites spectrum $E[N_k]=\theta/k$,

$E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\theta}{k}\left[1-f^{k}\right]
 =\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k$,
$\sum_{k}f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)<\infty$.

Hence

$\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}
 =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum_{k}f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]
 \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{p}\theta$

on the $M$ site set.  The $O(1)$ loss $ \theta\sum f^{k}/k$ is $o(a_{n})=o(\log n)$,
so the relative bias of the segregating-site count vanishes.  In the
arbitrarily large sample limit every true $p>0$ site retains at least one
unfiltered derived copy w.h.p. and $S_{obs}\to S_{true}$.

Thus on the ascertained variant-only site set $\theta_{W}$ is
asymptotically recovered by the MCAR loss + reference imputation, whereas
the frequency-weighted statistic $\pi$ is permanently down-shifted by the
$(1-f)$ thinning of derived allele counts.  The usual upward ascertainment
bias to polymorphic sites is common to both statistics and is not created by
the imputation step. Finite-$n$ the $f^{k}$ tail gives a small $O(1)$
downward finite-sample bias for $S$, but in the stated $n\to\infty$ limit

The site set that is actually analysed is the union of SNVs that are
present in the VCF.  Let $r=1-f\in(0,1)$ be the per-haplotype
retention probability for a true derived allele and $f>0$ the per-haplotype
filtering probability.  The reference allele is never lost.

For a true derived frequency $p>0$ on the ascertained set

$$p_{obs}=r\,p\qquad{\rm in\;expectation},$$

because a true derived copy is kept with probability $r$ and is
systematically turned into reference with probability $f$.  Hence for a
site

$$E\big[\,\pi_{i}^{obs}\,\big]=2p_{obs}(1-p_{obs})
     =2rp\bigl[1-rp\bigr]<2p(1-p)=\pi_{i}^{true},$$

and the attenuation $p\to rp$ persists for every $p$.  In particular

$$E\big[\hat\pi_{obs}\big]=E_{p}\!\left[2rp(1-rp)\right]
        <E_{p}\!\left[2p(1-p)\right]=\pi_{true},$$

so the pairwise-difference average is systematically depressed by the
reference imputation.  The bias is a frequency-weighted bias and does not
vanish as $n\to\infty$.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence of polymorphism.
A true segregating site with $k_{n}=2np>0$ derived copies in a sample of
$n$ diploids is scored as monomorphic after imputation iff all $k_{n}$
copies are filtered in the same realisation.  With independent MCAR loss

$$\Pr\{{\rm site\;lost}\mid p\}=f^{k_{n}}=f^{2np}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0,
\qquad\forall p>0,$$

and with the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’
condition the union VCF is the true set of segregating sites.  Hence

$$E[S_{obs}]=\sum_{k\ge1}E[N_{k}]\bigl[1-f^{k}\bigr]
          =\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k,$$

$a_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{2n-1}k^{-1}$.  $\sum f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)<\infty$ so
the loss is $O(1)$ whereas $a_{n}\sim\log n\to\infty$.  In the arbitrarily
large-sample limit

$$ \frac{S_{obs}}{a_{n}}=\theta_{W}^{obs}
   =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]\xrightarrow{p}\theta,
$$

i.e. on the ascertained SNV set $S_{obs}\xrightarrow{p}S_{true}$ and
$\theta_{W}^{obs}$ is asymptotically recovered.  The segregating-site
count is therefore first-order robust to random, allele-independent loss
followed by reference imputation, whereas the allele-frequency distortion
produced by the imputation makes $\pi$ persistently down-biased.

Upward ascertainment to the variant-only site set is common to both
statistics; conditional on the VCF site set the imputation step biases
$\pi$ downwards while $\theta_{W}$ is asymptotically unbiased.  This is
the usual presence-absence vs frequency-weighted distinction.

B. Only pi (nucleotide diversity) is biased by the reference imputation,
Watterson’s $\theta$ is asymptotically unbiased for the ascertained
site set.

With the VCF site set taken as the union of true segregating sites the
filtering is per haplotype MCAR with retention $r=1-f>0$ and reference
imputation

$Y_{i}=X_{i}{\bf1}_{\rm obs}$,  $ {\mathbb E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}]=rX_{i}$ ,

so that for a site with true derived frequency $p>0$

${\mathbb E}[\hat p\mid p]=rp<p$ .

* Segregation

A true site with $k=2np$ derived copies in the sample is seen as
segregating after imputation iff $K_{o}>0$ with $K_{o}\mid k\sim{\rm Bin}(k,r)$.
Hence

${\rm Pr}\{\hbox{site lost}\mid k\}=f^{\,k},\qquad
{\mathbb E}[S_{o}]=\sum_{i}\bigl[1-f^{\,k_{i}}\bigr]$.

On the infinite-sites spectrum ${\mathbb E}[N_{k}]=\theta/k$

${\mathbb E}[S_{o}]=\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k$,

$\sum_{k}f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)<\infty$, and

$\hat\theta_{W}^{o}=S_{o}/a_{n}
 =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum_{k}f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\theta$.

For every fixed $p>0$, $f^{\,2np}\to0$ so a truly segregating site is seen
as segregating w.h.p. in the $n\to\infty$ limit. Up to the usual VCF
ascertainment to variable sites the presence/absence information on which
Watterson's estimator is based is therefore asymptotically recovered.
The $O(1)$ loss $\theta\sum f^{k}/k$ is $o(a_{n})$ and vanishes relatively
as the sample is made arbitrarily large; in finite $n$ it is a small
downward $O(1/\log n)$ term.

* Pairwise diversity

${\mathbb E}[2\hat p(1-\hat p)\mid p]=2rp(1-rp)<2p(1-p)$ for $0<p<1$, and
with $p\ll1$ ${\mathbb E}[2\hat p(1-\hat p)\mid p]\simeq2rp$.
Hence on the ascertained site set

${\mathbb E}[\pi_{o}]={\mathbb E}_{p}[2rp(1-rp)]<{\mathbb E}_{p}[2p(1-p)]
=\pi_{\rm true},$

and in the rare-site limit ${\mathbb E}[\pi_{o}]\approx r\,\pi_{\rm true}$.
The $r$ attenuation of the observed allele frequencies persists as
$n\to\infty$: reference imputation systematically turns derived copies into
reference, depressing heterozygosity and pairwise differences by a
non-vanishing factor $r$, $1-f^{2}$ etc.

Thus on the union VCF site set $\theta_{W}=S/a_{n}$ is asymptotically
unbiased under random per-sample loss with reference imputation, whereas
$\pi$ is systematically downward biased by the allele-frequency shrinkage
$p\mapsto rp$. The usual VCF ascertainment bias to polymorphic sites is
common to both statistics. This is the classic robustness of $S$ to random
missing-as-reference versus the sensitivity of $\pi$ to frequency
distortion.

For a site with k true derived copies in the 2n haplotypes, after independent per-haplotype filtering with loss probability f>0 the number of derived copies that survive is Bin(k,1-f). The site is scored as segregating in the imputed alignment iff K_o>0, i.e. with probability 1-f^{k}. On the infinite-sites spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k,

E[S_obs]= Σ_{k≥1} θ/k [1-f^{k}] = θ a_n - θ Σ_{k≥1} f^{k}/k .

Σ f^{k}/k = -log(1-f) >0 is an O(1) constant. So

E[θ̂_W^{obs}] = E[S_obs]/a_n = θ [1 - ( -log(1-f))/a_n ] < θ

for every finite n. The loss is the rare-variant tail: sites with k=1,2,… are lost with probability f^{k}>0. E[π_i^{obs}] = 2p_obs(1-p_obs)=2(1-f)p[1-(1-f)p] < 2p(1-p)=π_i^{true}

for 0<p<1, with the usual rare-site approximation E[π_i^{obs}]≈2(1-f)p. The attenuation factor 1-f persists in the n→∞ limit; π is a frequency-weighted statistic and is systematically depressed by the reference enrichment.

E[S_obs]= Σ_{k≥1} θ/k [1- m^{k}] = θ a_n - θ Σ_{k≥1} m^{k}/k

E[\pi_{o}] =E_{p}\!\left[2rp(1-rp)\right] < E_{p}\!\left[2p(1-p)\right]
$$

for any $r<1$. The $(1-f)$ attenuation of the allele frequency is a
systematic reference bias. It persists as $n\to\infty$; $\pi$ is
consistently down shifted, $E[\pi_{o}]\to\theta(1-f^{2})<\theta$, and in
the rare-site regime $E[\pi_{o}]\simeq2r p$.

A site is scored by Watterson only on presence/absence of polymorphism.
For a true segregating site with $k_{n}=2np>0$ true derived copies

$$
\Pr\{{\rm site\;lost\mid p}\}= f^{\,k_{n}}=f^{\,2np}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0
\qquad\forall p>0 .
$$

With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the
union set is the true set of segregating SNVs, $ {\cal S}_{T}$.
Hence

$$
\Pr\{K_{o}>0\mid k\}=1-f^{k}\to1,\qquad
E[S_{o}]=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\theta}{k}\!\left[1-f^{k}\right]
       =\theta a_{n}-\theta\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{f^{k}}{k}.
$$

$\sum f^{k}/k=-\log(1-f)=O(1)$ while $a_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{2n}k^{-1}
\sim\log n\to\infty$. Thus

$$
\hat\theta_{W}^{o}=S_{o}/a_{n}
   =\theta\Bigl[1-\frac{\sum f^{k}/k}{a_{n}}\Bigr]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{P}\theta,
$$

so on the ascertained SNV set the segregating-site count, and hence
Watterson’s $\theta_{W}$, is asymptotically recovered. The $O(1)$
loss $ \theta\sum f^{k}/k$ is $o(a_{n})$ and vanishes relative to $S$
in the arbitrarily large sample limit. The usual upward ascertainment to
the variant-only site set is common to both statistics.

The frequency-dependent quantity $\pi$ is therefore the one that remains
systematically depressed by reference imputation, $\theta_{W}$ is first
order asymptotically unbiased on the VCF site set.

That is the B statement: only $\pi$ is biased, $\theta_{W}$ is
asymptotically unbiased for the ascertained sites.  The familiar finite-$n$
downward $O(1)$ loss of the rarest sites is the finite-sample bias that
is often quoted as “both biased’’ but vanishes relative to $a_{n}$ as
$n\to\infty$.
public_text.13:
I think the “asymptotically unbiased for θW” line is being pushed too far and it hides the finite-sample reality that the question is actually about.

The site set we analyse is the union VCF, so every site is genuinely segregating in the population. After per-sample quality filtering a true derived copy is kept with probability 1−f and turned into a forced reference call with probability f, independently per haplotype. For a site with k true derived copies in the sample

Pr[ site is seen as segregating after imputation | k ] = 1 − f^{k}.

With the infinite-sites spectrum E[N_k]=θ/k this gives

E[S_obs]= Σ_k θ/k [1− f^{k}] = θ a_n − θ Σ_k f^{k}/k .

Σ_k f^{k}/k = −log(1−f) < ∞, so the absolute loss of segregating sites is a positive constant. The relative loss θ Σ f^{k}/k / a_n vanishes as a_n∼log n→∞, but the question says “arbitrarily large” not infinite, and the loss is  non-zero for every finite n. In particular the rare-variant tail k=O(1) never disappears: for k=1,2,… Pr[loss]=f^{k}>0 persists no matter how large n is. Those rare variants are a substantial fraction of a human VCF and they are exactly the ones that can be wiped out when the few carriers that exist happen to be the haplotypes in which the site was filtered. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples” condition is about the union before per-sample deletion; after sample-specific deletion + reference imputation a site can still be imputed as reference in every haplotype and become monomorphic in the final alignment. That makes S systematically undercounted and θ_W = S/a_n downward biased in any real data set, which is the finite-N form that Colleagues 11 and 12 already flagged.

π is affected in a different but also systematic way. The observed derived frequency is E[p̂|p]= (1−f)p, so

E[2p̂(1−p̂)] = 2(1−f)p[1−(1−f)p] < 2p(1−p)

for every 0<p<1. The reference imputation therefore thins the allele frequency spectrum at every site and depresses the pairwise difference at every site. The attenuation to (1−f) of the frequency persists as n→∞.

So we have a genuine downward reference bias for the frequency-weighted statistic π and a downward loss-of-segregating-sites bias for the presence/absence statistic θ_W. On the VCF site set both estimators are underestimates of the true diversity for the population. That is the both-biased situation argued by Colleagues 13, 14, 2, 5 and 9.
public_text.18:
The sites that enter the analysis are the union $M$ of sites that are
segregating in the panel and are present in at least one sample after the
per-sample quality filter.  Let $r=1-m>0$ be the per-haplotype probability
that a true derived copy is retained and let $k_{i}=2np_{i}>0$ be the true
number of derived copies at a site $i$ in $2n$ phased haplotypes.  After
reference imputation

* $K_{o,i}\mid k_{i}\sim {\rm Bin}(k_{i},r)$,
* the site is seen as segregating iff $K_{o,i}>0$,

${\rm Pr}\{ {\rm site\;lost}\mid k_{i}\}=m^{k_{i}},\qquad
{\rm Pr}\{ {\rm site\;segregating}\mid k_{i}\}=1-m^{k_{i}}  .
$

For a fixed true frequency $p_{i}>0$
$m^{k_{i}}=m^{2np_{i}}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, so

${\rm Pr}\{ {\rm site\;segregating}\mid p_{i}>0\}\to1 ,$

and with the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’
${\rm E}[S_{obs}]=\sum_{i}[1-m^{k_{i}}]\to |M|$.  Hence on the ascertained
site set $M$

$S_{obs}\xrightarrow{p}S_{true},\qquad 
\hat\theta_{W}^{obs}=S_{obs}/a_{n}\xrightarrow{p}S_{true}/a_{n},$

up to the $O(1)$ loss $\theta\sum_{k}m^{k}/k=-\theta\log r$ which is
$o(a_{n})$.  Presence/absence of polymorphism is therefore recovered in
the $n\to\infty$ limit; Watterson’s estimator is asymptotically
unbiased for the $M$ site set.  The $O(1)$ loss for the very rare
$k=O(1)$ tail is the familiar finite-$n$ downward bias, $o(\log n)$,
and disappears in the arbitrarily large sample limit imposed here.

Frequency information is not recovered.  For a haplotype
$Y = X B$ with $B\sim {\rm Bernoulli}(r)$ independent of the true allele
$X\in\{0,1\}$,
${\rm E}[Y\mid X]=rX$ and

${\rm E}[\hat p_{i}\mid p_{i}]=r p_{i}<p_{i}$.

The observed per-site heterozygosity is therefore

${\rm E}\big[\,2\hat p_{i}(1-\hat p_{i})\mid p_{i}\big]
   =2r p_{i}\big[\,1-r p_{i}\big] <2p_{i}(1-p_{i}),$

with the attenuation $r$ persisting for every $p_{i}>0$.  In the
usual rare-site regime ${\rm E}[\hat\pi_{i}]\approx2r p_{i}$ so that

${\rm E}[\pi_{obs}]
   ={\rm E}_{p}\!\left[\,2r p(1-rp)\right]
   <{\rm E}_{p}\!\left[\,2p(1-p)\right]=\pi_{true},$

and the bias $1-r^{2}$ for $p\approx1/2$ does not vanish as $n\to\infty$.
Reference imputation therefore systematically depresses observed allele
frequencies and pairwise differences at every site.

Thus on the VCF ascertained site set the segregating-site count, and
hence Watterson’s $\theta_{W}$, is asymptotically recovered by random
allele-independent loss with reference imputation, whereas nucleotide
diversity $\pi$ remains consistently downward biased by the $r$
attenuation of allele frequencies.  The shared upward ascertainment bias
from restricting to $M$ is common to both statistics and is not created
by the imputation step.  In finite samples both statistics are mildly
downward biased by the $m^{k}$ tail, i.e. the classic $O(1)$ loss of the
rarest sites.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The data are the union VCF sites, “no completely missing SNV across all samples”, with per-haplotype MCAR loss of a true derived call with probability m>0 and reference imputation for missing calls. Reference alleles are never lost.

For a true haploid frequency p>0, observed frequency in expectation
E[ p̂ | p ] = (1-m)p < p.
Hence per site heterozygosity
E[ 2 p̂(1-p̂) | p ] = 2(1-m)p[1-(1-m)p] < 2p(1-p),
and for rare p E[π̂_i] ≈2(1-m)p.
The (1-m) thinning is per haplotype and does not vanish with n, so π̂ converges to E_p[2(1-m)p(1-(1-m)p)] ≠ E_p[2p(1-p)]. π is systematically downward biased, persistent as n→∞. This is agreed by all.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence. With k=2np true derived copies
Pr[site lost after imputation | k] = m^k,
Pr[site segregating] =1- m^k.
For fixed p>0, m^k = m^{2np} →0 as n→∞. With the union site set = true segregating set,
E[S_obs]= Σ_k θ/k [1- m^k] = θ a_n - θ Σ_k m^k/k,
a_n= Σ_{k=1}^{2n-1}1/k ~ log n, Σ_k m^k/k = -log(1-m)=O(1).
Thus S_obs/a_n = θ[1- O(1)/a_n] → θ in probability. On the ascertained VCF site set θ_W is asymptotically recovered; the O(1) loss of the k=O(1) tail is o(a_n). This is the “θ_W robust, π sensitive” argument made by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7.

The disagreement is finite vs asymptotic. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 stress the O(1) absolute loss -θ Σ m^k/k >0 persists for any finite n, and the k=O(1) rare-variant tail, which dominates S, has Pr[loss|k]=m^k>0 independent of n. With reference enrichment a truly segregating site can be imputed as reference/reference in the finished alignments even though it was present in the union VCF; thus in operational finite-sample terms both S and θ_W are downward biased, and π is downward biased. The “arbitrarily large” phrasing is interpreted as n→∞ limit by the majority, giving only π biased on the ascertained site set; the common VCF ascertainment to variable sites biases both statistics upward relative to the whole genome, but that bias is common and not created by the imputation.

The key unresolved nuance is whether the question intends the formal n→∞ limit, in which case the relative bias of θ_W vanishes while π’s attenuation persists, i.e. B, or the realistic finite-but-large-sample operational bias where the O(1) loss of rare sites makes θ_W also downward biased, i.e. C. My current understanding is the asymptotic statement is the intended one: only π remains systematically biased; θ_W is asymptotically unbiased for the union SNV set, with only a vanishing O(1)/log n finite-sample downward bias.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The data generation is MCAR per-haplotype loss of a true derived call with per-site per-haplotype filter probability f>0, retention r=1-f, followed by deterministic reference imputation. On a true site p>0

E[ p̂ | p ] = r p < p

so for a pair

Pr[Y_i≠Y_j]=2 r p [1- r p] < 2p(1-p).

Hence E[π̂_i]=2 r p[1- r p] is systematically < 2p(1-p). With n→∞ E[π̂]→E_p[2 r p(1-r p)]≠E_p[2p(1-p)], a persistent downward allele-frequency attenuation. The bias does not vanish with sample size; for rare sites E[π̂]≈2 r p. This is the classic missing-as-reference frequency bias.

Pr[site lost after imputation | k]=f^{k},  Pr[segregating]=1-f^{k}.

With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the union site set is the true segregating set. Under infinite sites E[N_k]=θ/k

E[S_obs]= Σ_k θ/k [1-f^{k}] = θ a_n - θ Σ_k f^{k}/k,
 Σ_k f^{k}/k = -log(1-f)=O(1), a_n=Σ_{1}^{2n-1}1/k ~ log n.

Hence S_obs/a_n = θ[1- Σ f^{k}/k / a_n] → θ in probability as n→∞. For every fixed p>0, f^{2 n p}→0, so a truly segregating site is seen as segregating w.h.p. Majority in the round: Colleagues 10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 argue B, only π biased, θ_W asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained set. Colleagues 13,14,5,2,9 argue C, both biased, emphasizing the O(1) absolute loss of the k=O(1) rare-variant tail and that in any finite realisation reference imputation can turn a rare site monomorphic, giving E[S_obs]<S_true and E[θ_W]<θ. 11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The per-haplotype mechanism is random thinning of derived alleles with deterministic reference fill-in for the missing calls.

Let per-haplotype loss prob be m>0, retention r=1-m. For true derived frequency p>0 on the ascertained SNV set

E[hat p | p]= r p < p

and for an imputed allele Y = X B with B~Bern(r)

E[1_{Y1 != Y2}] = 2 r p (1 - r p) < 2p(1-p).

Hence per site heterozygosity is attenuated to 2rp(1-rp) and the sample mean
pi_obs converges to E_p[2rp(1-rp)] != E_p[2p(1-p)]. The attenuation persists as n→∞ because r<1 is a fixed per-sample filter. Systematic downward bias of nucleotide diversity.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence. A true segregating site with k=2np derived copies is seen as monomorphic after imputation iff all k copies are filtered: Pr[lost|p]= m^k. For any fixed p>0, m^{2np}→0 as n→∞. With the stated “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ the union site set is the true segregating set. Hence S_obs →P S_true and θ_W,obs = S_obs/a_n → S_true/a_n. With infinite-sites E[S_obs]=θ a_n -θ Σ f^k/k, with Σ f^k/k = -log(1-f)=O(1) while a_n~log n. Relative bias of θ_W vanishes as n→∞; the O(1) loss is the finite-sample loss of the k=O(1) tail.

Thus on the ascertained VCF site set θ_W is asymptotically robust to MCAR loss+reference imputation whereas π remains systematically depressed by the r thinning. The VCF ascertainment to variable sites biases both statistics upwards relative to genome-wide, but that bias is common.

Disagreement in the room: colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 stress the finite-sample reality: for k=O(1) the loss probability f^k>0 persists, the expected absolute loss of S is θ Σ f^k/k>0, and with a substantial minority filtered per sample rare variants can be wiped out in the realised imputed alignment, so both S and π are downward biased in any finite, however large, sample. Colleagues 1,10,11,15,16,17,18 and 3,4,6,7 argue the relative bias of S/a_n is o(1) and that in the arbitrarily large-sample limit stated the only first-order distortion introduced by filter+reference imputation on the union SNV set is the frequency attenuation of π.

Current belief: in the n→∞ limit stipulated, only π is persistently biased; Watterson’s estimator is asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained SNV set, with a small O(1)/a_n finite-sample downward bias that vanishes relatively. That is the B statement: only nucleotide diversity is biased by reference imputation; θ_W is asymptotically unbiased for the ascertained site set. For a true haploid derived frequency p>0
E[p̂]=r p < p
so per site heterozygosity is attenuated:
E[2p̂(1-p̂)] = 2 r p [1 - r p ] < 2p(1-p).

Pr[site lost after imputation | k]= f^k,
Pr[site seen segregating | k]=1-f^k.

E[S_obs]=∑ θ/k [1-f^k]= θ a_n - θ ∑ f^k/k,
∑ f^k/k = -log(1-f)=O(1) while a_n=∑_{1}^{2n-1}1/k ~ log n →∞.

reflection_text.6:
The data are the union VCF sites, “no completely missing SNV across all samples”, with per-haplotype MCAR loss of a true derived call with probability m>0 and reference imputation for missing calls. Reference alleles are never lost.

For a true haploid frequency p>0, observed frequency in expectation
E[ p̂ | p ] = (1-m)p < p.
Hence per site heterozygosity
E[ 2 p̂(1-p̂) | p ] = 2(1-m)p[1-(1-m)p] < 2p(1-p),
and for rare p E[π̂_i] ≈2(1-m)p.
The (1-m) thinning is per haplotype and does not vanish with n, so π̂ converges to E_p[2(1-m)p(1-(1-m)p)] ≠ E_p[2p(1-p)]. π is systematically downward biased, persistent as n→∞. This is agreed by all.

Watterson depends only on presence/absence. With k=2np true derived copies
Pr[site lost after imputation | k] = m^k,
Pr[site segregating] =1- m^k.
For fixed p>0, m^k = m^{2np} →0 as n→∞. With the union site set = true segregating set,
E[S_obs]= Σ_k θ/k [1- m^k] = θ a_n - θ Σ_k m^k/k,
a_n= Σ_{k=1}^{2n-1}1/k ~ log n, Σ_k m^k/k = -log(1-m)=O(1).
Thus S_obs/a_n = θ[1- O(1)/a_n] → θ in probability. On the ascertained VCF site set θ_W is asymptotically recovered; the O(1) loss of the k=O(1) tail is o(a_n). This is the “θ_W robust, π sensitive” argument made by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7.

The disagreement is finite vs asymptotic. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 stress the O(1) absolute loss -θ Σ m^k/k >0 persists for any finite n, and the k=O(1) rare-variant tail, which dominates S, has Pr[loss|k]=m^k>0 independent of n. With reference enrichment a truly segregating site can be imputed as reference/reference in the finished alignments even though it was present in the union VCF; thus in operational finite-sample terms both S and θ_W are downward biased, and π is downward biased. The “arbitrarily large” phrasing is interpreted as n→∞ limit by the majority, giving only π biased on the ascertained site set; the common VCF ascertainment to variable sites biases both statistics upward relative to the whole genome, but that bias is common and not created by the imputation.

The key unresolved nuance is whether the question intends the formal n→∞ limit, in which case the relative bias of θ_W vanishes while π’s attenuation persists, i.e. B, or the realistic finite-but-large-sample operational bias where the O(1) loss of rare sites makes θ_W also downward biased, i.e. C. My current understanding is the asymptotic statement is the intended one: only π remains systematically biased; θ_W is asymptotically unbiased for the union SNV set, with only a vanishing O(1)/log n finite-sample downward bias.

Hence per-site heterozygosity is attenuated by the r thinning and the attenuation is frequency dependent. For rare sites E[π̂]≈2rp, for common sites the bias is ~1-r². The reference imputation systematically enriches alignments for the reference allele, so 

E[π̂] = E_p[2rp(1-rp)] < E_p[2p(1-p)] = π_true

and the bias persists as n→∞ because E[p̂]=rp for every site. π is therefore persistently downward biased on the VCF ascertained site set.

Presence/absence is different. For a site with k=2np true derived copies

Pr{ site seen as monomorphic after imputation | k}=f^k ,  Pr{segregating}=1-f^k.
